lesson.title: One Curve to Rule Them All: Standardizing Any Normal Distribution
lesson.summary: The standard normal curve is the one normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and standardization is the process of converting any normal value into a z-score so that every normal distribution can be analyzed using this single curve.
lesson.body:
The 68-95-99.7 rule only answers questions at exact whole-number distances from the mean. Most real questions do not land so conveniently, so statisticians rely on a single reference curve, the standard normal curve, which is simply the one specific normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Because every normal distribution shares the same underlying bell shape and differs only in its mean and standard deviation, any value from any normal distribution can be converted onto this one standard curve, and every question about it can then be answered using tools built for that single curve alone.

The conversion is called standardization, and it produces a value called a z-score, calculated with a simple formula: z equals the value x, minus the mean mu, divided by the standard deviation sigma. A z-score measures how many standard deviations a value sits above or below the mean of its own distribution: a positive z-score means the value is above the mean, a negative z-score means it is below the mean, and a z-score of 0 means the value equals the mean exactly. Once converted to a z-score, a value has effectively been relocated onto the standard normal curve, stripped of the original units and the specific mean and standard deviation it came from.

Suppose a student scores 85 points on a test where the class mean is 75 and the standard deviation is 5 points. That student's z-score is (85 minus 75) divided by 5, which equals 10 divided by 5, or 2. A z-score of 2 says the student's score sits exactly two standard deviations above the mean, matching the 68-95-99.7 rule's language directly and confirming this student scored among the higher performers in the class.

Standardization becomes especially powerful when comparing values from two completely different distributions. Suppose a student scores 650 on the SAT, where scores are approximately normal with a mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 100, and a different student scores 29 on the ACT, where scores are approximately normal with a mean of 21 and a standard deviation of 5. Converting both to z-scores: the SAT score gives z equal to (650 minus 500) divided by 100, or 1.5, while the ACT score gives z equal to (29 minus 21) divided by 5, which is 8 divided by 5, or 1.6. Even though 650 and 29 are numbers from entirely different scales and cannot be compared directly, their z-scores can: the ACT score's z of 1.6 is slightly higher than the SAT score's z of 1.5, meaning that student performed marginally better relative to their own test's population.

This is the whole point of building a standard normal curve in the first place: rather than building a separate reference for every possible mean and standard deviation, every normal distribution can be translated into z-scores and analyzed using one single, universal curve. The next step is learning to read that universal curve using a normal table, which converts a z-score into an exact probability rather than the rough estimates the empirical rule provides.
